44.history: The pit town where the Abhainn uaine leaves the hills was the heart of the crews' own long resistance. The eleven days of its great strike in the seventy-seventh year won what the crews could win, and its roll kept Sìneag's search for an old law of rest. Its Comann an Adhlacaidh became Faire nan Lòchran, which kept a purse, a book and the copies of every petition; Eilidh nic Raghnaill led a crew there and kept the book. A' Chompanaidh walled its pithead, and in the first days of the war its constables held the walls eleven days until the well ran dry, and were marched to the coast unharmed on Eilidh's word. Sìol-lann na Companaidh built there against a stoppage was the first on the hill, and the overseer's clerk who copied the forbidden song kept his copy in its roll. Its boats have been launched at the landing since before any roll.

355.history: The coal-breakers' mill town west of the silver country grew so crowded with the guild's refiners and carters in the eighty-second year that it was called by the silver town's name from then on, and the rolls speak of the old town and the new without always saying which. It lived on the carrying trade between the two. It began as a coal-breaking mill for the diggings in the hills east of the capital, and the carters of both towns shared one inn and one quarrel for the rest of the age.

502.history: Where Rathad na Mèinne from the eastern diggings met the mills, silversmiths settled in the eighties and worked the guild's bar into brooches, clasps and buckles for the humans' own market. Theirs was the one craft of the island sold across the sea under its own name. It stands at the meeting of Rathad na Mèinne and the mills with a citadel above it, and its smiths' marks were known in the humans' shops across the sea.

20.history: The river port of the north-central country and heart of the hawk-faithful asked Teachdaireachd na h-Eaglaise for a copy of Wren's grammar in the thirteenth year, to read what the humans wrote of them; of all the copies that survive, theirs bears the most notes in the margins. In the war Buidheann an t-Seabhaig Luaidhe slept a night in a byre near it on the road to Oirthir an t-Seabhaig. It lies on the Abhainn ìseal, and its hawk-priests kept that copy in the temple where anyone who could read the humans' letters might ask to see it.
20.known_for: the most-read copy of Wren's grammar

269.history: The damp hill of the north-west heard of An Togail as a rumour before it came as a list. In the high summer of the ninetieth year An Togail's officers took its masons, Dùghall Clachair and his crew of six, to build the tower at Baile chrom, and their small fields stood untilled that year. Dùghall cut the names of his crew into the lintel of the lamp-room, the only writing on any of the five towers. It is the market of the country of the two Muileann àrsaidh, and An Togail's officers came to it again in each of the three years the towers were building.

95.history: The harbour of the great strait in the far north-west, near where the strangers first raised the land, took the first tally of An Togail, when the officers read the names of the chosen from a list in the humans' tongue and took the wrong son. The custodians wrote the names again in Dia-thìris, that they might know whom to look for. Its grief was loud and short, as a first grief is. Its yards took timber for A' Chompanaidh's hulls, and An Togail's officers used its quay as their first station in the north-west.
